title: Eating out — ordering and asking
title_target: আমার এক কাপ চা চাই — a-mar èk kap cha chai
goal: Order food, ask for things, and use the second verb form ending in -তে — the key to saying “want to eat”, “can go” and “start learning”.
bekal: ask with আমার … চাই and আমার … লাগবে
use the -তে form: খেতে, যেতে, করতে, দেখতে
combine it with চাই (want) and পারি (can)
name the Bengali dishes that turn up on the table most often

dialogs.title: কথোপকথন — At a small eatery
dialogs.intro: Rahim takes Ani to lunch at a small eatery near his office. Watch the two verb forms working as a pair: খেতে চাই, যেতে পারি, দেখতে চাই.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: What would you like to eat? The fish curry is good here.
lines.literal: what — to-eat — want? here — fish's — curry — good.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: I'd like fish. But not too spicy.
lines.literal: I — fish — to-eat — want. but — more — spicy — don't.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Okay. Brother, two rice and one plate of fish curry.
lines.literal: right — is. brother, two — rice, one — plate — fish's — curry.

lines.speaker: ওয়েটার:
lines.id: Shall I give you dal? There's bhorta today.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: What's bhorta? I'd like to see it.
lines.literal: bhorta — meaning — what? I — to-see — want.

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Vegetables roasted and then mashed. Like Indonesian sambal.
lines.literal: vegetable — roasting — mashing — make. Indonesia's — sambal's — like.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Then I want bhorta! And I need a glass of water.
lines.literal: then — my — bhorta — wanted! and — one — glass — water — will-be-needed.

lines.speaker: ওয়েটার:
lines.id: Sure. I'll make it less spicy, don't worry.
lines.literal: okay. spice — less — will-give, worry — will-do — don't.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Thank you. Can I eat with my hands?
lines.literal: thanks. I — hand — with — to-eat — can?

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: Of course! We all eat with our hands.

lines.speaker: আনি:
lines.id: Oh, in Indonesia we eat with our hands too!

lines.speaker: রহিম:
lines.id: See? We're just the same. Eat up, before it gets cold!

notes: **The second verb form ends in -তে, and it works like English “to …”.** খাওয়া (to eat) → **খেতে**; যাওয়া (to go) → **যেতে**; করা (to do) → **করতে**; দেখা (to see) → **দেখতে**; পড়া → **পড়তে**. This form never stands alone; it always pairs with a second verb that carries the person ending.

**Three pairs cover almost every A1 need:** … **তে চাই** (want to …), … **তে পারি** (can …), … **তে হয়** (have to …). আমি যেতে চাই (I want to go), আমি যেতে পারি (I can go), আমাকে যেতে হয় (I have to go). ⚠️ The order is the reverse of English: the main verb comes **first** and the helper **last** — Bengali's habit of putting the deciding word at the end.

⚠️ **চাই has two faces, and both are correct.** If what you want is a **thing**, the person takes the possessive form: **আমার চা চাই** (I want tea — literally “my tea is wanted”). If what you want is an **action**, you use the plain form: **আমি খেতে চাই** (I want to eat). English uses one word “want” for both; Bengali changes the structure.

**লাগবে means “will be needed” and very often stands in for “I need”.** আমার এক গ্লাস পানি লাগবে (I need a glass of water), আমার দশ মিনিট লাগবে (I need ten minutes), কী লাগবে? (what do you need?). ⚠️ The person is always in the possessive form — আমার, আপনার — never আমি.

**ঝাল governs your whole eating experience in Bengal.** ঝাল কম দিন (less spicy, please), ঝাল ছাড়া হবে? (can it be made without chili?), একটু ঝাল ভালো (a little spicy is nice). ⚠️ “A little spicy” in Bengal may be more than you expect, so say so early. What surprises visitors even more, though, is the **sweetness** of the desserts.

**Eating with your hand is the custom, not a fallback** — and it's always the right hand. Rice is mixed with the gravy using the fingertips, then pushed into the mouth with the thumb. ⚠️ If you ask “may I eat with my hand?”, your host will be pleased; asking shows you're paying attention.

**খেয়ে যান — “eat before you go” — is an invitation you'll hear often**, and turning it down flatly feels cold. If you really can't, answer **আজ না, পরে খাব** (not today, I'll eat next time) or accept at least a cup of tea. In Bengal, refusing food entirely is almost like refusing the hospitality itself.

after: **The negative attaches to the second verb, not the first:** আমি যেতে চাই **না** (I don't want to go), আমি খেতে পারি **না** (I can't eat). ⚠️ Don't put না in the middle.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three things at a Bengali table
items: **The meal has an order.** At a traditional feast, dishes come in sequence: bitter first (শুক্তো), then vegetables, then fish, then meat, and sweets last. If you eat everything at once, no one will scold you — but follow the order and your host will be impressed.

**আরেকটু নিন — “have a little more” — will be said again and again.** It isn't empty politeness; refusing once counts as good manners, and only a third refusal is taken seriously. Safety line: **আর পারব না, সত্যি!** (honestly, I can't eat any more).

**Tea is served in small glasses and usually already sweetened.** If you don't want sugar, say so from the start: **চিনি ছাড়া** (*chi-ni chha-Ra* — without sugar). Once the tea is poured, it's too late.

blocks.text: One word worth keeping: **অতিথি** *ôtithi* — guest. Bengali culture has the saying **অতিথি নারায়ণ** — “the guest is a god”. In practice it's simple, and you'll feel it soon: the home you visit will give you more food than you ask for, refuse your money, and feel you haven't really visited until you've eaten. The best response is to accept happily, praise the cooking with **খুব মজা হয়েছে**, and return the favor by bringing something next time.
